Series::is_floating_point¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

bool Series::is_floating_point() const

What It Does¶

Returns true when the Series’ dtype is a real floating-point format — Float16, BFloat16, Float32, Float64, or one of the two 8-bit float formats — and false for integers, Bool, and complex.

It is a dtype test that reads dtype().is_floating() and nothing else. The content of the tensor is irrelevant: a Float64 tensor full of NaN and inf is still is_floating_point() == true, because the storage format is what is being asked about, not the values in it.

The one boundary that surprises people is complex. Complex64 is a pair of Float32 lanes and Complex128 a pair of Float64 lanes — the components are floats — but the scalar category is complex, so is_floating_point() returns false for them. The correct test for “any continuous real-or-complex numeric data” is therefore:

x.is_floating_point() || x.is_complex()

is_floating_point() alone silently drops complex input.

Across every scalar type, the three category predicates behave as:

dtype

is_complex

is_floating_point

is_signed

Bool

false

UInt8 … UInt64

false

false

false

Int8 … Int64

Float16, BFloat16, Float32, Float64, the 8-bit floats

false

Complex64, Complex128

false

true

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

bool true for the real floating formats, false for integer, Bool, and complex dtypes.

Gradient¶

Not applicable — is_floating_point() returns a plain bool.

Examples¶

Example 1. Only the real float formats answer true — integers, Bool, and complex all answer false.

for (auto st : {pluss::ScalarType::Bool, pluss::ScalarType::Int32,
                pluss::ScalarType::Float16, pluss::ScalarType::Float32,
                pluss::ScalarType::Float64, pluss::ScalarType::Complex64}) {
  auto x = pluss::series::zeros({1}, st);
  std::cout << x.dtype() << " -> is_floating_point=" << std::boolalpha
            << x.is_floating_point() << "\n";
}

Output¶

bool -> is_floating_point=false
int32 -> is_floating_point=false
float16 -> is_floating_point=true
float32 -> is_floating_point=true
float64 -> is_floating_point=true
complex64 -> is_floating_point=false

Float16 and BFloat16 both count — a routine that hand-checks only Float32/Float64 would wrongly reject half-precision input, which is exactly the mistake is_floating_point() exists to prevent.

Example 2. Complex is excluded even though its components are floats; the || is_complex() idiom brings it back in.

auto f = pluss::series::zeros({1}, pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
auto c = pluss::series::zeros({1}, pluss::ScalarType::Complex128);
auto i = pluss::series::zeros({1}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "float64  continuous? " << (f.is_floating_point() || f.is_complex()) << "\n"
          << "complex128 continuous? " << (c.is_floating_point() || c.is_complex()) << "\n"
          << "int64    continuous? " << (i.is_floating_point() || i.is_complex()) << "\n";

Output¶

float64  continuous? true
complex128 continuous? true
int64    continuous? false

Example 3. Content never changes the answer — a tensor of NaN and inf is still floating-point.

auto x = pluss::make_series({std::nan(""),
                             std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity(),
                             0.0});
std::cout << "has NaN and inf, is_floating_point=" << std::boolalpha
          << x.is_floating_point() << "\n";

Output¶

has NaN and inf, is_floating_point=true

To ask about the values, use isnan, isinf, or isfinite; is_floating_point() is purely about the format.

Example 4. An integer literal builds an integer Series; is_floating_point() reports that, and to is what changes it.

auto i = pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3});
std::cout << "i.dtype()=" << i.dtype()
          << " is_floating_point=" << std::boolalpha << i.is_floating_point() << "\n";
auto f = i.to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
std::cout << "after to(Float64): is_floating_point=" << f.is_floating_point() << "\n";

Output¶

i.dtype()=int64 is_floating_point=false
after to(Float64): is_floating_point=true

Reverse-mode autodiff needs a floating dtype — tracks_slope_ on an integer Series has nothing to accumulate into. is_floating_point() is the guard before enabling gradient tracking on data of unknown provenance.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Complex is not floating-point. Use is_floating_point() || is_complex() whenever complex input should also be accepted.

  • Bool is neither floating, complex, nor integral (see dtype) — a “floating vs. integral” branch has a third case it must not forget.

  • The answer is format-only. NaN/inf/0 content is irrelevant; use the is* value predicates for that.

  • Half formats (Float16, BFloat16) and the 8-bit floats all count — don’t reimplement this check by enumerating dtypes by hand.

Summary¶

is_floating_point() is a dtype-category predicate:

  • true for the real float formats (Float16 through Float64 and the 8-bit floats), false for integer, Bool, and complex

  • metadata-only — NaN/inf content does not change it

  • complex is excluded despite having float components; add || is_complex() for an “any continuous data” test

  • the standard guard before enabling reverse-mode autodiff

  • Series::is_complex / Series::is_signed: the other two category predicates.

  • Series::isnan / Series::isinf / Series::isfinite: the value-level questions is_floating_point() does not answer.
